terms.definition: The freshness of the wine — what makes you salivate and reach for another sip. Higher in cool climates.
The percentage of alcohol in the total volume of the wine.
The process in which yeasts consume grape sugar and produce alcohol, CO₂ and heat.
A delimited area with its own rules: permitted grape varieties, maximum yield per hectare and minimum ageing.
The label on the back of the bottle, where the grape variety, the producer and the tasting notes usually live.
A white wine made from black grapes, pressed without contact with the skins.
The sense of weight and density of the wine in the mouth: light, medium or full.
A fungus that dehydrates grapes on the vine and concentrates sugar and aroma. The basis of sweet wines such as Sauternes and Tokaji.
Gentle pressing of black grapes, whose juice already runs pink. A rosé method.
A wine with little or no residual sugar. Dry is the opposite of sweet, not the opposite of flavourful.
Wine with grape spirit added, ending up at 15–22% alcohol. Port, Madeira and Sherry are fortified.
The skin of the grape, where the colour, the tannins and much of the aroma live.
A grape distillate used to fortify wine. It is usually neutral and high in alcohol.
A type of grape within the species Vitis vinifera — Chardonnay, Touriga Nacional, Merlot.
The picking of the grapes, and also the time of year when it happens.
A sweet wine made from grapes frozen on the vine: the water stays behind as ice crystals in the press and what runs out is a highly concentrated juice.
Grapes picked beyond the normal point of ripeness, with more concentrated sugar.
Contact between the juice and the skins, which extracts colour, tannin and aroma.
The wine resting before bottling, in stainless steel, concrete, amphora or barrel.
Grape juice before and during fermentation, still with little or no alcohol.
Wine regions outside Europe — the Americas, Oceania, South Africa. The label leads with the grape variety.
A wine blending harvests from different years to keep a consistent house style. Common in sparkling and fortified wines.
A wine between dry and sweet: the sugar is noticeable but discreet.
The historic wine regions of Europe and the Mediterranean. The label leads with origin, not with the grape.
A white wine fermented in contact with the skins, gaining amber colour and tannin. It is the subject of module 14.
Extracting juice from the grapes under pressure. For whites it happens before fermentation; for reds, after.
Sugar left in the wine because fermentation did not consume all the sugar in the must.
Drawing off part of the juice from a red fermentation early on: that juice becomes rosé, and the red left behind gains concentration.
An extra fermentation carried out in a sealed container — bottle or tank — which traps the CO₂ and creates the bubbles.
A few hours of contact with the skins, used to make rosé. It is the most common rosé method.
Wine with bubbles, from CO₂ dissolved under pressure.
Wine without bubbles, usually between 8% and 15% alcohol.
A preservative and antioxidant used in nearly every wine; fermentation itself already produces some. The label warning is compulsory above a minimum threshold and does not signal poor quality.
Wine with noticeable residual sugar, from a stopped fermentation or from very concentrated grapes.
A compound from skins, seeds and oak. Not a flavour but a texture: the dry, rough feeling in the mouth typical of red wines.
The combination of soil, climate, altitude, aspect and human tradition of a place — and the mark it leaves on the wine.
The year the grapes were picked — not the year of bottling or of sale.
The vine species behind almost every wine in the world. It contains thousands of grape varieties.
A drink obtained exclusively from the alcoholic fermentation of fresh grape juice.
The microorganism that turns grape sugar into alcohol and CO₂. It can be ambient, from the vineyard itself, or selected in a laboratory.
